Emma Tucker
 
How Dolly Parton Built an Empire on Owning Her Songs
 
Plus, Kevin Warsh puts a September rate hike in play, and the strongest El Niño in a generation wreaks havoc on the global economy
 
 
ALAMY STOCK PHOTO
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Dolly Parton was thrilled when Elvis Presley wanted to record “I Will Always Love You.” Then she learned he wanted half the songwriting profits, even though he had nothing to do with the composition. Parton walked away from that deal. It was an early example of the business savvy that powered an empire spanning music, movies and Dollywood. She was fiercely protective of her songwriting catalog at a time when even the Beatles and Rolling Stones failed to maintain control. As the world remembers Parton, one of our top stories today looks at how her business instincts made her a shrewd operator in the notoriously opaque music industry.

 

For a final taste of summer, follow along as reporter Jen Rose Smith takes an eating tour of Maine’s Damariscotta River, where oyster season is just hitting its peak. She spent two days sampling her way through one of the state’s greatest concentrations of oyster farms, each with its own distinct taste.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The U.S. has rushed so many munitions to fight Iran that military planners worry it is diminishing America’s ability to defend against potential threats from China and Russia, U.S. officials said.

 

• The U.S. reached a deal with Venezuela to secure control of a big chunk of the Latin American country’s oil reserves.

 

• The pharma industry is entering its biggest wave of patent expirations in more than a decade. Nearly every company has at least one blockbuster drug going off patent in the next five years.

 

• By some estimates, China’s oil reserves last year exceeded those in the U.S. by nearly 600 million barrels, giving Beijing a critical defense against the West as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets.

 

• As his approval ratings sag, President Trump is focused on burnishing his legacy, but Republicans worry that focus could backfire with voters and threaten their control of Congress.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh’s growing concern about inflation put a September interest-rate increase in play, sending bond yields higher and stocks lower.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The Epstein scandal set off a power struggle at one of Wall Street’s biggest firms.

 

When Leon Black announced his retirement as CEO of the financial behemoth Apollo Global Management in January 2021, he was hoping for a clean succession. But the announcement came the same day as the release of an independent report that found Black had paid Jeffrey Epstein $158 million for financial advice over five years. Two months later, Black was out of the job early, and he would come to blame his messy downfall on one of his closest associates, Josh Harris. In this excerpt from “Money to Burn: The Unvarnished Truth About Leon Black, Apollo, and the Rise of a New Wall Street,” William D. Cohan details the crisis behind the scenes at Apollo as the Epstein scandal unfolded.

 

5.

 

The strongest El Niño in a generation is wreaking havoc on the global economy.

 

Scientists monitoring data from satellites and ocean buoys declared the onset of El Niño in June. It is shaping up to be among the strongest in living memory, and its effects are already rippling around the world. The weather phenomenon is showing up in the cost of passing through the Panama Canal and in Chilean copper output, and might influence everything from Asia’s rice crop to the powder at Colorado ski resorts. Ed Ballard and Costas Paris explain where the shock waves are hitting and what could come next.

6. SEE THE STORY

 
 
Farmers pick grapes at a winery near Yinchuan, China. QILAI SHEN FOR WSJ
 

An unlikely wine region is winning over sommeliers.

 

Emma Gao started growing Cabernet Sauvignon in the sandstorm-swept foothills of China’s Ningxia region in 2007. Now, her wines are being poured at restaurants from New York to London, as sommeliers look to entice drinkers bored by Bordeaux and Barolo with new wine experiences. Take a look inside the vineyard behind China’s boutique-wine boom.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

 

• Saturday: The Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole wraps up. Iceland holds a vote on whether to restart talks on joining the EU. College football’s Week Zero continues with a slate of kickoff games.

 

• Sunday: The 2026 U.S. Open begins its main draw in Flushing Meadows.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$352,000
 

That’s the price of a one-year-old BMW X5 at a dealership in Singapore. For the past 36 years, a firm cap on car ownership has kept the city-state largely free of gridlock. But prices for the certificates required to put a car on the road have hit new highs, forcing drivers to make tough choices about whether to still own a vehicle.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Schools are banning phones. Are students actually paying more attention?

 

More than two-thirds of states now require school districts to restrict phone use. A study found that the bans are effective at curbing phone use, and by the second year, schools saw fewer disciplinary problems and improved student well-being. Family & Tech columnist Julie Jargon looks at whether those benefits extend to student attention and academic performance.
